blocks.content: A .env file holds a whole set of environment variables in one place, KEY=VALUE per line, loaded in one shot instead of a long list of individual -e flags.
A .env file is about as simple as configuration gets, one KEY=VALUE pair per line, no quoting complexity, no nesting, easy to read and easy to generate from a script.

blocks.alt: One variable per line, nothing more

blocks.content: --env-file reads every line of the file and sets each one as an environment variable in the container, exactly as if you had typed a -e flag for each, without actually typing them all.

blocks.alt: A whole file of variables, loaded with one flag

blocks.content: 3. Where This Shows Up Constantly: Docker Compose
blocks.text: 3. Where This Shows Up Constantly: Docker Compose

blocks.content: Docker Compose (covered in its own dedicated module) automatically looks for a .env file in the same directory as your docker-compose.yml and loads it without any explicit flag at all, which is why .env files are such a common sight in Compose-based projects.

blocks.alt: Compose picks this up automatically, no flag needed

blocks.content: 4. Keep It Out of Version Control
blocks.text: 4. Keep It Out of Version Control

blocks.content: When a .env file holds real credentials (database passwords, API keys), it belongs in .gitignore, never committed to the repository, exactly the same principle covered in the .dockerignore topic for keeping secrets out of a build context, applied here to source control instead.

blocks.alt: Real secrets never belong in a committed .env file

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A .env file is a simple KEY=VALUE list, loaded in bulk with --env-file instead of many individual -e flags.
Docker Compose loads a .env file automatically, and any file holding real credentials should always be excluded from version control.
